connection: Earlier sessions added focused tests when assertions were the natural verification tool. This session names and standardizes the testing practice already in use. Organize the permanent test suite around Arrange–Act–Assert and add missing PayrollService behavior coverage.
objectives: Identify the Arrange, Act, and Assert sections of the real PayrollServiceTests.cs, even though the source file has no comments marking them.
Explain why the test mocks IClockEntryRepository with a configured .Setup(...).Returns(...) but mocks IEmployeeService with no configuration at all.
Compute by hand why two shifts of 2 and 3 hours produce the asserted total of 5.0, tracing through GetEmployeeClockEntries and GetDuartion().
Write a second, independent test for a boundary case CalculateTotalHours does not yet cover, such as an employee with zero completed entries.

visuals.title: Arrange builds the scenario
visuals.explanation: Two ClockEntry objects are constructed and clocked out, then a mocked repository is configured to return them for employee 1.

visuals.title: Act calls exactly one method
visuals.explanation: CalculateTotalHours(1, DateTime.MinValue, DateTime.MaxValue) is the single call under test.

visuals.title: Assert checks one observable value
visuals.explanation: Assert.Equal(5.0, totalHours, precision: 5) checks the sum, not any internal implementation detail.

visuals.title: An unconfigured mock is itself evidence
visuals.explanation: Mock<IEmployeeService>() with no .Setup() calls proves, in the test's own structure, that PayrollService's IEmployeeService dependency is not exercised by this code path.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does the real test configure repository.Setup(r => r.GetEmployeeClockEntries(1, DateTime.MinValue, DateTime.MaxValue)).Returns(...) with those exact arguments?
options: Moq only returns the configured value when the mocked method is called with matching arguments -- CalculateTotalHours must call GetEmployeeClockEntries with exactly DateTime.MinValue and DateTime.MaxValue for the test to work
The arguments are arbitrary and any values would work
DateTime.MinValue and DateTime.MaxValue are required by xUnit
preQuiz.explanation: Moq's Setup matches by argument value -- the test's Act call and the Setup's expected arguments must agree for the stub to fire.

preQuiz.prompt: Why is employeeService a Mock<IEmployeeService>() with no .Setup() calls at all?
options: PayrollService's constructor requires an IEmployeeService argument to exist, but CalculateTotalHours never calls any of its members, so no behavior needs to be configured
The test is incomplete and missing required setup
preQuiz.explanation: This is the real, deliberate shape of the test -- it proves the dependency is currently unused by simply never telling the mock what to do.

preQuiz.prompt: 2 hours + 3 hours = 5.0 -- which two real method calls produce those numbers?
options: GetDuartion().TotalHours on each of the two mocked ClockEntry objects, summed by CalculateTotalHours's .Sum() call
The Mock<IClockEntryRepository> computes the sum internally
preQuiz.explanation: Each ClockEntry's real GetDuartion() computes ClockOut - ClockIn; CalculateTotalHours's real Sum call adds the two TotalHours values together.

concept.title: Arrange creates only relevant state
paragraphs: Construct the entries and repository behavior the test needs. Deterministic timestamps keep the expected total obvious.
Shared mutable setup makes failures harder to diagnose, so each test owns its arrangement.

concept.title: Act performs one behavior
paragraphs: The Act phase calls the behavior named by the test. If several unrelated actions are required, the test may be describing too much.
Async tests await the operation rather than blocking on Result.

concept.title: Assert checks an observable outcome
paragraphs: Assert the returned total or persisted state, not private implementation details.
A failing assertion should explain which behavior changed.

lab.objective: Organize the permanent test suite around Arrange–Act–Assert and add missing PayrollService behavior coverage.
lab.startingCondition: Earlier sessions added focused tests when assertions were the natural verification tool. This session names and standardizes the testing practice already in use.
steps: Create ClockEntryTests and identify its Arrange, Act, and Assert responsibilities without adding noisy comments.
Create PayrollServiceTests for completed entries, open entries, and no entries.
Use deterministic dates and avoid sharing mutable fixtures between tests.

commit: session-28: teach unit tests and arrange act assert
review: The lab uses tests because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: If CalculateTotalHours were changed to call _employeeService.RenameService somewhere, what would happen to the existing PayrollServiceTests.cs test as written today?
options: It would likely throw, since Mock<IEmployeeService>() with no setup returns default/null behavior for any called member -- the test would need a real .Setup() added
Nothing -- Moq automatically implements every member with sensible behavior
The test would automatically update itself
postQuiz.explanation: An unconfigured mock is not a no-op stand-in for every possible future call -- it only behaves correctly for the calls the test author anticipated.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does the test use At(9), At(11), At(13), At(16) instead of DateTime.Now for the shift times?
options: Deterministic, fixed timestamps make the expected duration (2 hours, 3 hours) exact and reproducible on every test run
DateTime.Now cannot be used inside a Mock setup
At() is required by xUnit's [Fact] attribute
postQuiz.explanation: A test that depended on DateTime.Now would have a different 'now' every run -- fixed offsets from DateTime.Today keep the math exact and repeatable.

postQuiz.prompt: What would a new test for 'an employee with one still-open (not clocked out) entry' need to configure differently?
options: GetEmployeeClockEntries would need to return only completed entries -- matching the learner solution's own ClockOut != null filter -- so the open entry should simply not appear in the mocked return value
The test would need to catch an exception from CalculateTotalHours
PayrollService would need a different constructor
postQuiz.explanation: The real GetEmployeeClockEntries already filters out open entries before PayrollService ever sees them -- the mock should reproduce that same real filtering behavior, not rely on CalculateTotalHours to filter again.

reflections: Why is an unconfigured Mock<IEmployeeService> itself evidence about PayrollService's current behavior, not just an incomplete test?
What would you need to change about this test if PayrollService's constructor parameter order were swapped?
How does testing against interfaces (IClockEntryRepository, IEmployeeService) rather than concrete classes make this test possible without an EF Core database?
whatBreaks: Configuring Mock<IEmployeeService> with unnecessary .Setup() calls would not break the test, but it would misrepresent the real dependency as used when it is not -- exactly the kind of drift Session 20's dead-dependency discussion warns about. Using DateTime.Now instead of the fixed At(hour) helper would make the expected duration nondeterministic. Asserting on an internal field instead of the public totalHours return value would couple the test to PayrollService's implementation instead of its contract.
summary: PayrollServiceTests.cs is the learner solution's one real xUnit test: Arrange builds two genuine ClockEntry shifts behind a configured Mock<IClockEntryRepository>, Act calls CalculateTotalHours once, and Assert checks the single resulting total -- while its unconfigured Mock<IEmployeeService> is itself proof that PayrollService's second dependency is not yet exercised.
